title: Make the error alert fire and the log archive land on the share

blocks.text: The on-call alert reads the application log and pages someone for every error line. Last night the payment gateway timed out forty times and nobody was paged. The same morning the log archiver reported that the share for host `web-07` doesn't exist, although the file server team can see it.
`LogAlerts` already filters the log; what it filters with, and where it archives to, are the two `TODO`s in `src/main/java/practice/LogAlerts.java`:

items: `errorWord()`: the pattern that finds `ERROR` as a word of its own, so `ERRORS` or `NOERROR` don't count;
`shareFor(host)`: the UNC path of a host's nightly logs, which for `web-07` is `\\web-07\logs\nightly` exactly as the file server team wrote it.

blocks.text: When you're done, a line such as `03:10 ERROR timeout` raises the alert, and the archiver gets a path the file server recognises. About two lines in total.

cases.says: a log with no error in it raises no alert
the share path names the host and its logs folder
a line that holds ERROR as a word of its own is picked out for the alert
ERROR inside a longer word, such as ERRORS, is not an error line
the share path starts with two backslash characters, as a UNC path does
every folder name of the share path arrives as written, with no control character in it

origin.section: Every Quote and Backslash Is Written Twice, and a Wrong Backslash Can Still Compile

concepts: Inside a traditional literal every quote and backslash meant for the text is written with a backslash in front, so text for another language that has escapes of its own (JSON, regex, a Windows path) carries two layers.
Only escapes javac doesn't know are errors; a single backslash before t, n, b, r, f or s compiles and silently puts a control character or a space into a path or a regex.
